sources.title: The Ideas behind the English Opening
English Opening, Anglo-Indian Defense 1...Nf6 (A15) (search snippet only)

overview: 1.c4 Nf6 is a crossroads, not a single structure. Black develops a piece, covers e4 and d5, and waits to see whether White wants d4 (which usually transposes into the King's Indian, Nimzo-Indian, Queen's Indian or Grünfeld) or a pure English set-up. The main branches are 2.Nc3 (with ...e6 giving Nimzo or Hedgehog-type play, ...g6 a King's Indian set-up, ...d5 a reversed Grünfeld, ...c5 or ...e5 symmetrical or reversed-Sicilian structures), 2.g3 and 2.Nf3. The typical English middlegame is a manoeuvring game with White's pressure on d5 and queenside space against Black's central break (...d5 or ...e5), but 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 (Mikėnas-Carls) can be sharper. Black's choice of branch decides almost everything about character and structure.

white_ideas.idea: Fianchetto the king's bishop (g3, Bg2) and pressure d5 and the long diagonal (Staunton-style set-up with Nc3, g3, Bg2, e3).
Take the centre with e4 against ...e6 or ...g6 (Mikėnas-Carls with 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4; 2.Nc3 g6 3.e4 heads for a King's Indian or avoids the Grünfeld).
Play d2-d4 at the right moment to open the game, or transpose into an Indian Defence if Black allows it.
Queenside expansion with Rb1 and b4 (this is the theme sources attach to symmetrical English structures; not found stated for Anglo-Indian specifically).

black_ideas.idea: Wait: develop Nf6 and decide on a structure (Nimzo-style ...e6/...Bb4, King's Indian ...g6/...Bg7, Queen's Indian, Grünfeld) after seeing White's set-up.
Strike in the centre with ...d5 (reversed Grünfeld, 2.Nc3 d5) or ...e5 (reversed Sicilian type).
Hedgehog-type set-up (2.Nc3 e6, ...b6, ...d6, ...a6) with later ...b5 or ...d5 breaks against White's c4/e4 space.

typical_structures.structure: Indian Defence structures after d4 (King's Indian, Nimzo-Indian, Queen's Indian, Grünfeld).
Hedgehog (Black pawns a6, b6, d6, e6) against White pawns on c4/e4, a Maróczy-type bind.
Reversed Sicilian / reversed Grünfeld type positions with White c4 and Black pawn on e5 or d5.

character.notes: Overall moderately forcing at most: Exeter says positions are moderately forcing, with maneuvering battles over tactics; Wikibooks calls it a solid, flexible defence. The Mikėnas-Carls (2.Nc3 e6 3.e4) is the exception and can lead to forcing tactical play. The Hedgehog branch is solid-but-cramped rather than sharp. Character depends on which branch Black picks.

gambit.notes: No material is given in the root or main lines.

soundness.notes: Fully sound. Wikipedia: the English Opening is considered reliable and flexible; world championship players (Botvinnik, Petrosian, Karpov, Kasparov, Carlsen, Ding Liren) have used the English. 1...Nf6 is the most common reply to 1.c4. No claim that either side is worse.

structure.notes: Not one answer: root is a crossroads. If White plays d4 the game becomes an Indian Defence (semi-open or closed centre depending on branch). 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 or 2.Nc3 g6 3.e4 give a White centre. Hedgehog branch has Black pawns on a6/b6/d6/e6 against c4/e4 (partly open d-file, centre not locked). The typical English with ...d5 or ...e5 breaks gives tension in the centre with pawns kept on for a time rather than early central pawn trades.

approach.notes: Played at the very top: 1.c4 Nf6 is the most common reply to the English, which is the fourth most popular first move and one of the four most successful (Wikipedia). It is a reply to 1.c4, not a fixed set-up played against everything, but Black's flexibility (waiting to choose the structure) is its identity. Wikipedia and Exeter describe the English as flexible and usable as a transposition tool.

level.notes: Little forced theory at move 2 because Black chooses the structure, so the burden is knowing plans in whichever Indian, Hedgehog or reversed-Sicilian structure arises. Black must know enough of the King's Indian, Nimzo-Indian, Queen's Indian and Grünfeld if White transposes with d4. Hedgehog requires sophisticated handling per Wikipedia. Studying Black's side, a player needs a repertoire answer to 2.Nc3, 2.g3 and 2.Nf3.

plan_phrases: queenside expansion with Rb1 and b4

sublines_that_differ.name: Mikėnas-Carls Variation
sublines_that_differ.how: White takes the centre immediately; can lead to forcing tactical positions (sharper than the English norm).

sublines_that_differ.name: Hedgehog System
sublines_that_differ.how: Black builds a compact a6/b6/d6/e6 structure and waits for ...b5 or ...d5; solid but cramped.

sublines_that_differ.name: King's Indian set-up
sublines_that_differ.how: 3.e4 transposes to the King's Indian; 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2 is the English fianchetto version.

sublines_that_differ.name: Reversed Grünfeld
sublines_that_differ.how: Black strikes at once for the centre; open and tactical compared with quiet English lines.

description.claim: The Anglo-Indian is a flexible response to the English.
description.note: Black keeps all options open and decides the structure after White commits.

description.claim: It immediately challenges White's control of d5.
description.note: Nf6 covers d5 and e4 and prepares ...d5; White's c4 pawn aims at d5 as well, so the knight contests rather than takes the square.

description.claim: Black often transposes into King's Indian, Queen's Indian or Grünfeld depending on White's set-up.
description.note: Also Nimzo-Indian. Transposition mostly happens when White plays d4.

description.claim: It leads to a complex positional game where plans and pawn structures matter more than memorising sharp tactical lines.
description.note: True for the main English lines; the Mikėnas-Carls (3.e4) and ...d5 lines are more forcing.

common_plans.claim: White completes a kingside fianchetto (g3, Bg2) and controls d5.
White often expands on the queenside with Rb1 and b4.
common_plans.note: Sources tie Rb1/b4 to symmetrical English structures; not found for Anglo-Indian specifically. Own understanding: plausible in the 2.Nc3 g6 3.g3 lines.

common_plans.claim: Black stays flexible by choosing an Indian set-up.
Black challenges the centre with a timely ...d5 or ...e5.
common_plans.note: Reversed Grünfeld and reversed Sicilian ideas.

common_plans.claim: A common dynamic is White's queenside pressure versus Black's counter-strike in the centre or on the kingside.
common_plans.note: Plausible but no source states it for this root.
